topic: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Reflection of waves (physics only)
subject: physics

items.q: A sound wave travelling through the air reaches a thick concrete wall. Which statement best describes reflection at this boundary?
items.correct: Some of the sound is sent back into the air it originally came from
items.misconception: Reflection cannot occur here, as concrete is not polished
items.why: Reflection is nearly always introduced using a plane mirror, so students attach the property to the mirror rather than to the boundary. A clear image needs a smooth surface, but reflection itself does not. Sound echoes from a rough brick wall and light reflects from matt paper; both are reflections at a boundary.
items.random_wrong: All of the sound must pass on into the concrete and travel through

items.q: A lamp lights a plane mirror and a sheet of white paper equally. A clear image is seen in the mirror but not in the paper. Why is this?
items.correct: The smooth mirror keeps parallel rays parallel when they reflect
items.misconception: The rough paper scatters rays and so breaks the law of reflection
items.why: Students see the scattered result and conclude the rule has broken down, because they picture the surface as flat rather than as many tiny tilted facets. Draw the rough surface magnified as a set of small flat facets. Each facet obeys the law of reflection with its own normal, and the different facet directions are what scatter the rays.
items.random_wrong: The paper absorbs every ray of light that arrives at it

items.q: A radio wave meets a thick metal sheet and is absorbed. What happens to the energy that the wave was carrying?
items.correct: It is transferred to the thermal energy store of the metal
items.misconception: It is destroyed, so less energy exists than there was before
items.why: Everyday language such as 'the sound died away' suggests disappearance, and absorption is often taught only as the wave stopping. Energy is conserved. Absorption is a transfer, not a loss: a black car roof in sunlight and the warm foam in a sound-proofed room are both evidence of where the energy went.
items.random_wrong: It is stored inside the wave until that wave is set free again

items.q: Light from a street lamp shines on a clean window and carries on into the room beyond. Which word describes what the light has done at the glass?
items.misconception: The light has been absorbed by glass
items.why: Everyday language such as 'the sound died away' suggests disappearance, and absorption is often taught only as the wave stopping. Energy is conserved. Absorption is a transfer, not a loss: a black car roof in sunlight and the warm foam in a sound-proofed room are both evidence of where the energy went.
items.random_wrong: The light has been reflected away

items.q: A narrow ray of light travels through air and meets the flat surface of a glass block. Which statement about this boundary is correct?
items.correct: Some light is transmitted into the glass and some is reflected back
items.misconception: All the light is transmitted, because the glass is transparent
items.why: Textbook diagrams usually show a single arrow for a single process, and questions often name just one effect, so students treat them as mutually exclusive. You can see your own faint reflection in a window while also seeing the street through it, and the glass warms slightly. That one boundary is reflecting, transmitting and absorbing at the same time.
items.random_wrong: All the light is absorbed, since the glass warms up a little

items.q: You are drawing a ray diagram for light reflecting from a plane mirror. From which line is the angle of incidence measured?
items.correct: From the normal, drawn at right angles to the mirror surface
items.misconception: From the mirror surface, at the point where the ray lands on it
items.why: The surface is already drawn and obvious, while the normal has to be added by the student, so it feels like an optional extra. The two angles add up to 90°, so a ray at 30° to a mirror has an angle of incidence of 60°. Draw the dashed normal first and measure everything from it.
items.random_wrong: From the reflected ray, measuring back to the incident ray

items.q: A ray strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 30°. What is the angle of reflection, and from where is it measured?
items.correct: 30°, measured from the normal on its other side
items.misconception: 60°, measured from the normal, since they total 90°
items.why: Students mix the angle measured from the normal with the angle measured from the surface, and subtract from 90° out of habit. The law of reflection is angle of reflection = angle of incidence, with both measured from the normal, so 30° in gives 30° out.
items.random_wrong: 30°, measured from the surface of the mirror

items.q: Which feature must appear in a correctly drawn ray diagram showing reflection at a plane mirror?
items.correct: Arrows on the rays to show the direction
items.misconception: A dashed normal drawn along the mirror surface
items.why: Students remember only that the normal is dashed, and copy the dashing onto the most prominent line already in the diagram. 'Normal' means perpendicular. Check every diagram with a set square: the normal must make 90° with the surface at the point of incidence.
items.random_wrong: The image marked in front of the mirror surface

items.q: A matt black metal plate and a shiny silver metal plate are left side by side in bright sunlight. Why does the black plate become hotter?
items.correct: It absorbs more of the light, transferring that energy to its thermal store
items.misconception: It reflects more of the light, and reflection is what warms a surface
items.why: Students associate 'more happening at the surface' with heating, and reflection is the process they can see, so they credit it with the warming. Reflected energy leaves the surface again and cannot warm it. Only absorbed energy is transferred into the material, which is why solar absorbers are matt black.
items.random_wrong: Black surfaces transmit the sunlight straight through into the metal

items.q: Heavy fabric curtains are drawn across a window facing a busy road, and the room becomes noticeably quieter. Which effect best explains this?
items.correct: The soft fabric absorbs much of the sound that reaches it
items.misconception: The curtain reflects all the sound waves straight back
items.why: Students know a hard wall echoes and assume any barrier works by bouncing sound away, without distinguishing hard surfaces from soft ones. Hard smooth surfaces reflect sound and produce echoes; soft porous ones absorb it. That is why recording studios are lined with foam and not with tiles.
items.random_wrong: The curtain lowers the frequency below what ears detect

items.q: In Required practical activity 9 a ray box is aimed at a plane mirror, then at gloss card, then at matt card. Which quantity must be kept the same throughout?
items.correct: The angle of incidence of the ray from the box
items.misconception: The kind of surface that the ray box is aimed at
items.why: Students confuse the control variable with the independent variable, and the surface is the thing the question tells them to think about. The surface is the independent variable, the reflected ray is the dependent variable, and the angle of incidence is the control variable that must be held constant.
items.random_wrong: The angle of reflection read off the protractor

items.q: In Required practical activity 9 a ray of light is shone from air into a rectangular glass block, meeting the surface at an angle to the normal. What is seen as the ray enters the block?
items.misconception: It bends away from the normal
items.why: The 'towards' and 'away' rules are memorised as a pair and are easily swapped when the direction of travel is not checked. Slower means towards the normal. Entering glass the ray bends towards the normal; leaving the block back into air it bends away from it, so the emerging ray is parallel to the original one.

items.q: Why does a transmitted ray of light change direction as it enters a glass block?
items.correct: Because the light changes speed at the boundary; entering glass it slows down, and if it meets the boundary at an angle to the normal it bends towards the normal.
items.misconception: The light bends because glass is heavier or denser and physically pushes the ray sideways.
items.why: The word 'dense' is used loosely in everyday speech, so students reach for a mechanical push instead of a change of wave speed. Refraction is a wave speed effect. The part of the wavefront that reaches the glass first slows first, which swings the whole wavefront round and changes the direction of the ray.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A ray of light meets a glass block along the normal. What happens to its direction?
items.correct: It carries straight on without changing direction, although it does slow down inside the glass.
items.misconception: It still bends towards the normal, because light always refracts when it enters glass.
items.why: Students learn 'light bends towards the normal entering glass' as an unconditional fact and apply it even when the angle of incidence is zero. At an angle of incidence of 0° the whole wavefront reaches the boundary at the same instant, so there is nothing to swing it round. The speed changes but the direction does not.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where should the image be marked on a ray diagram for a plane mirror?
items.correct: Behind the mirror, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.
items.misconception: The image sits on the front surface of the mirror, where you see it.
items.why: The reflecting surface is where the light appears to come from, so students place the image on the glass rather than behind it. Extend the reflected rays backwards as dashed construction lines. They meet behind the mirror, and that meeting point is where the image is.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
